primary.title: State Department Title VIII Research Program Loses Federal Funding in 2013
primary.description_short: The State Department’s Title VIII program for Eurasian and Eastern European language training and research lost its FY2013 appropriation.
primary.description_medium: In 2013, the State Department’s Title VIII program for language training and research in Eurasian and Eastern European studies did not receive an appropriation for the federal fiscal year ending September 30. Contemporary reporting said the loss reduced fellowships and grants available in 2013–14. The evidence does not connect this Obama-era funding decision to Donald Trump.
primary.description_long: In October 2013, Inside Higher Ed reported that Title VIII, a State Department program supporting language training and research in Eurasian and Eastern European studies, did not receive an appropriation for the federal fiscal year ending September 30. The Association for Slavic, East European and Eurasian Studies said the absence would reduce fellowships and grants available in 2013–14. The article reported that Title VIII funding averaged about $4.5 million annually in the early 2000s and had been cut to $3.3 million in fiscal year 2012. A 2014 PONARS Eurasia republication of Alexander Gabuev’s Guardian article says State Department leadership decided in fall 2013 not to allocate money for Russian studies after Congress changed the relevant budget wording from “shall” to “may.” Together, the reports support a narrow account of a 2013 funding decision. They do not support the original claim that cuts continued through 2015 to shift resources toward Syria, ISIS, and gun violence. The decision predates Donald Trump’s presidency, and the evidence reviewed establishes no connection to him. Whether this unrelated Obama-era event belongs in a Trump-focused collection remains an editorial scope question.

frozen_original.title: Trump Fires All US Attorneys, Replaces with Loyalists Overnight
frozen_original.synopsis: In an unprecedented purge of the Justice Department, Trump fired all sitting U.S. Attorneys on his first night back in office and replaced them with handpicked loyalists by dawn. While new presidents occasionally change U.S. Attorneys, the speed and totality of the overnight replacement was unprecedented in modern history. The replacements bypassed the traditional Senate confirmation process in many districts through the use of interim appointments. Legal experts warned the action transformed federal prosecution from a nonpartisan function into a political weapon. The move set the stage for weaponized prosecutions of Trump's perceived enemies.

primary.title: Trump Said He Instructed DOJ to Terminate Remaining Biden-Era U.S. Attorneys
primary.description_short: Reuters reported that Trump instructed DOJ to terminate remaining Biden-era U.S. attorneys; the evidence does not show an overnight firing and replacement of all 93.
primary.description_medium: On February 18, 2025, Trump said he had instructed the Justice Department to terminate all remaining Biden-era U.S. attorneys, Reuters reported. He said the department had been “politicized like never before” and posted that the administration must “clean house” immediately. Reuters also described earlier termination notices and departures. This supports a reported instruction, not the original claim of a first-night purge or loyalist replacements by dawn.
primary.description_long: Reuters reported that on February 18, 2025, President Donald Trump said he had instructed the Justice Department to terminate all remaining Biden-era U.S. attorneys. Trump said the department had been “politicized like never before” and wrote that the administration must “clean house” immediately and restore confidence. Reuters said the White House had sent termination notices the previous week to several U.S. attorneys appointed by Joe Biden, while several others announced departures and others had left government. The corrected event is Trump’s reported instruction and its stated target, not a completed firing of every U.S. attorney. The supplied record does not support its original claim that all 93 sitting attorneys were fired on January 20 and replaced by dawn. Reuters did not report a nationwide roster of loyalist replacements in this account. The article distinguishes the February statement from the earlier transition: some attorneys received notices, while others announced or had already made departures. This entry preserves what Reuters reported Trump said and does not claim that DOJ completed every termination, that the action bypassed Senate confirmation, or that a court found the instruction unlawful.

Trump described the department as politicized and called for it to “clean house.” Reuters reported that the White House had sent termination notices the prior week to several Biden-appointed U.S. attorneys. Other attorneys announced departures, while some had already left government. The report therefore supports a public instruction directed at the remaining Biden-era attorneys and separate notices or departures involving some prosecutors. It does not establish that every U.S. attorney was removed, that all 93 were fired on January 20, or that loyalist replacements were installed by dawn. The article also does not show that the instruction bypassed Senate confirmation or that a court ruled it unlawful. The original entry’s first-night purge and replacement claims should not be retained. The event is the reported February instruction; its implementation and any effects remain unresolved.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends Student Loan Forgiveness Programs — Borrows Default Wave
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed executive orders dismantling Biden-era student loan forgiveness programs including the SAVE income-driven repayment plan that had provided lower monthly payments and eventual forgiveness for millions of borrowers. Borrowers who had arranged their finances around SAVE's terms were suddenly thrown into limbo as the program was frozen. Servicer call volumes spiked to unprecedented levels as millions of borrowers struggled to understand their new obligations. The administration also revoked the Department of Education's authority to broadly cancel student debt, ending multiple ongoing forgiveness initiatives for defrauded students, public servants, and disabled borrowers. An estimated 8 million borrowers who had received relief under Biden-era programs faced potential clawback of discharged debt.

primary.title: Eighth Circuit Affirms and Widens Injunction Against the SAVE Rule
primary.description_short: On February 18, 2025, the Eighth Circuit affirmed and widened a preliminary injunction against the federal SAVE student-loan repayment rule.
primary.description_medium: On February 18, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction in litigation over the federal SAVE student-loan repayment rule. It remanded the case with instructions to extend the injunction to the full rule and a related hybrid rule. This court ruling, rather than a January 20 Trump executive order ending forgiveness, is the event documented by the supplied record and court opinion.
primary.description_long: On February 18, 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued an order in appeals arising from challenges to the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) repayment rule. The court affirmed a district court’s preliminary injunction and remanded the case with instructions to modify that injunction so it covered the entire SAVE Rule and a related hybrid rule. The opinion describes a dispute brought by seven states, which argued that the Education Department exceeded its authority by allowing loan forgiveness through an income-contingent repayment plan; those are the states’ claims, not a final factual finding about borrower harm or misconduct. The federal officials, including the president in his official capacity, had appealed the preliminary injunction. This entry records the appellate court’s procedural ruling and its stated scope. The supplied record does not support its original assertion that Trump ended multiple forgiveness programs by executive order on January 20, that servicer calls spiked, or that eight million borrowers faced clawbacks. The court document also does not establish the later outcome of the litigation.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The origin of the dispute is a rule promulgated by the Department of Education to modify a pre-existing income contingent repayment (ICR) plan for federal student loans. This ICR plan, called Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE), altered payment thresholds, stopped interest accrual, and forgave loan balances after as little as ten years of repayment. Seven states challenged the SAVE Rule as exceeding statutory authority given to the Secretary of Education because they claim the Secretary cannot forgive loans through an ICR plan, among other things. The district court concluded they were likely to succeed on this claim and preliminarily enjoined the rule’s early loan forgiveness provisions. The parties filed cross-appeals. The Secretary of Education, Department of Education, and the President (collectively, federal officials) seek vacatur of the preliminary injunction, while the states request we broaden the injunction.
